chunks: Single-FET bidirectional level shifter. The question: Design a single-FET level shifter (passives are allowed).
This shifter translates an open-drain line, such as I²C, between two supply voltages using one small N-channel transistor and two pull-up resistors.
It works in both directions with no direction pin. Whichever side pulls the line low, the transistor passes that low to the other side.
When both sides let go, each side rises to its own supply.
Picture two balloons, each held up by its own air pump, at different pressures. A pinch valve between them opens whenever either balloon is squeezed flat.
Squeeze one and the other deflates too; let go and each re-inflates to its own pump's pressure. The pumps are the pull-up resistors.
The picture only holds for open-drain devices: a chip that actively drives its line high would fight the other side.
The gate is wired to the low rail V L. The source (bottom pin) faces the low-voltage line and the drain (top pin) faces the high-voltage line.
The body diode points from source to drain. Each side has its own pull-up.
Rail: a supply line, such as the 3. 3 volts or 5 volts rail. NMOS transistor: a voltage-controlled switch.
It turns on when its gate pin is more than about 1 volts above its source pin. Body diode: a one-way path built into the transistor, running from its source to its drain.
Open-drain: a device that can only pull a line low, never drive it high. Pull-up resistor: the resistor from a line to its own rail that makes the high level.
Tie the transistor's gate to the 3. 3 volts rail, its source to the 3. 3 volts line and its drain to the 5 volts line, with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up on each side.
Idle, the gate-to-source voltage is 0, so the transistor is off. If the 3. 3 volts side pulls low, the source drops, the gate-to-source voltage becomes 3.
3 volts, and it turns on, pulling the 5 volts side low. If the 5 volts side pulls low first, the body diode drags the source to about 0.
7 volts, so the gate-to-source voltage is 2. 6 volts and the transistor turns on. That is the whole idea.
"One N-channel FET, gate to the low rail, source on the low-voltage side, drain on the high-voltage side, and a pull-up on each side to its own rail.
Idle, Vgs is zero so it's off. If the low side pulls down, Vgs becomes the low rail and the FET pulls the high side down.
If the high side pulls down, the body diode drags the source down to 0. 6 volts, Vgs rises above threshold, and the FET finishes the job.
It's bidirectional but only for open-drain signals like I²C."
